title: Your study
tomorrow: a pantry wall quotes Jesus. why does it sound so familiar to Amira?

cards: A shopping cart, or a wishlist, holding six books on a subject you've just fallen for. A month later, one of them has a bookmark on page twelve. Wanting everything at once is a fast way to finish nothing.
So with too many books and one semester, which one do you pick? The Qur'an gives the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ a one-line prayer for exactly this hunger.

teach.b: Here it is, in Pickthall's words: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Increase. Not: give me all of it by Friday.
It's a direction more than a destination: more than yesterday, again tomorrow. A hadith in Sahih Muslim makes the road itself sacred.
The Prophet said that whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, God makes easy for them a path to Paradise. A road, walked, step by step.

And the Qur'an asks a question that honors anyone on it: "Are those who know equal with those who know not?" So what does ongoing study look like in a real week, with classes or a job already eating the hours?
The old picture is a student and a teacher working through one book together, finishing it, then opening the next. Some start with a short classic, like al-Nawawi's Forty Hadith, a hadith at a time.
Some take a single surah with a commentary beside it.

teach.h: ONE BOOK, ONE TIME, ONE PERSON.
teach.b: The pattern holds either way: one book, a regular time for it, and a person to ask when you get stuck, because I don't know needs somewhere to go.
One for tonight: the Qur'an's prayer for knowledge asks for more, never for all.

how: Muslims who want to keep learning join study circles at mosques, weekend classes or online courses, or read with a teacher, sometimes working through one classic text at a time.

games.q: your friend starts a coding course, a language app and a guitar course in the same week. by Sunday she's behind on all three and asks you what to drop. what fits today?
o: keep all three. pushing through is how you grow fastest.
keep one, with a set time and someone to ask, and finish it first.
drop all three until she has a free summer.
games.why: increase, not everything: one book, one time, one person to ask. the road is walked a step at a time.

practice: Stand up and walk slowly for a minute or two, inside or out. As you walk, ask yourself the one question about faith, or about life, you'd most like answered. Let that question choose your one book.
